parts:
Well, it hasn’t been the most elegant process. Basically my proposing something
to little response then my implementing it to everyone complaining about one thing
or another with no constructive alternatives. Hence everything moving glacially.

At the moment the writer is stuck in pull request limbo, and given that no one has
picked up I’m going to have to put off the ODE stuff and do it this week. Because
that’s all written and needs only be split up into a million pull requests, the only to
do is to update the interfaces (other than CmdStan which is already ready in a
branch).

Then there is the refactoring of the var_context. This will require lots of work
but I need to get it into a working state first, which will require the writer be done
to avoid some nasty merge conflicts. Once we start on this again there will be
plenty to help with.

Once that’s done we have to figure out how to implement the new flat arguments
(let’s all complain that we don’t like the current set up but not write a new one!),
especially validation methods for the interfaces.

Finally at that point we can implement a slew of new features blocked by the
lack of a consistent API and then define an output file specification consistent
with the API I/O routes. Given that spec we can write a robust csv_reader,
and all kinds of fancy bits like streaming data formats and streaming estimators.

So the immediate to dos are sparse
1) Propagate the new writer callback through the VB code and get it to compile.
2) Wait for all of this to be merged into Stan and then help update the interfaces.

I've already looked over the code under (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/1546) so I get what the overall goal is. Any suggestions about what the needs are for that branch at the moment?

parts: Just a couple comments:

On Mon, Sep 14, 2015 at 7:56 AM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
On Monday, September 14, 2015 at 5:55:16 AM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Well, it hasn’t been the most elegant process.  Basically my proposing something
> to little response then my implementing it to everyone complaining about one thing
> or another with no constructive alternatives.  Hence everything moving glacially.

That isn't why it's moving glacially. The reason most things get into the code base slowly is because pull requests are usually too big on construction, have problems, and are really not ready to go into the code as-is. There are plenty of pull requests that move quickly because they're easy to review, easy to verify, and they're ready to go (or close) when submitted.

Most proposals are fine, but proposals and implementation are different. When we start reviewing implementation, we actually look through and make sure it's not just correct but also something that can be maintained going forward.

Thanks for taking the time to sketch out where things are at, I appreciate it's frustrating to move something this big.  I don't have much of an immediate response to this but it does help with reading the code.  I do have two questions below.

> At the moment the writer is stuck in pull request limbo, and given that no one has
> picked up I’m going to have to put off the ODE stuff and do it this week.  Because
> that’s all written and needs only be split up into a million pull requests, the only to
> do is to update the interfaces (other than CmdStan which is already ready in a
> branch).

Is the right CmdStan branch the update_to_write_callback or issue-151-remove-writer?  It would probably help me understand what's going on if I have an  example to go by on the interface side.
The update_to_write_callback is where we want to get. issue-151-remove-writer is a much narrower scoped pull request. Check stan-dev/math#151

> Then there is the refactoring of the var_context.  This will require lots of work
> but I need to get it into a working state first, which will require the writer be done
> to avoid some nasty merge conflicts.  Once we start on this again there will be
> plenty to help with.

When you say "need to get [var_context] into a working state", does that mean that it's not in use?  I thought I saw it in CmdStan and rstan interface code. Could you elaborate a little more about that bit?
Michael's got some updates to the var_context that should make things much easier. It'll conflict with the writer interface change to the api.

> Once that’s done we have to figure out how to implement the new flat arguments
> (let’s all complain that we don’t like the current set up but not write a new one!),
> especially validation methods for the interfaces.
>
> Finally at that point we can implement a slew of new features blocked by the
> lack of a consistent API and then define an output file specification consistent
> with the API I/O routes.  Given that spec we can write a robust csv_reader,
> and all kinds of fancy bits like streaming data formats and streaming estimators.

+1 for streaming I/O!

Ok, but there are deeper issues here. Right now, the var_context is immutable, so it's easy to think about the instantiated model class as really exposing a function:
p(x, theta)
where x is truly fixed and is data.

We then take that instantiated model and do things assuming that this is true and that:
p(theta | x) \propto p(x, theta)

But... what happens when data is streaming and mutable? Then every call to p(x, theta) isn't really that what we thought it was.

I have no problem with it, but I do think we need to make it clear when data is fixed and when data is not. We've always assumed in our code that data is fixed, but once we change that, we'll need to rethink how we handle var_contexts.

Anyway, thanks again for clarifying what's going on, it really helps to understand the C++ API and where it's going.

parts: > Is the right CmdStan branch the update_to_write_callback or issue-151-remove-writer? It would probably help me understand what's going on if I have an example to go by on the interface side.
update_to_writer_callback will the eventual state of CmdStan.

> When you say "need to get [var_context] into a working state", does that mean that it's not in use? I thought I saw it in CmdStan and rstan interface code. Could you elaborate a little more about that bit?

See https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/feature/refactor_io_reader_writer

The idea is for the interfaces to create all var_contexts externally and then
pass them into the API. In order to get randomized inits this requires changing
the way the var_contexts are accessed, in particular factoring out all of the
transformations hidden in io_reader and io_writer.

This requires a ton of changes, and this branch never compiled because
I got to the point where making it work would conflict with the changes
in the writer.

Very wide .csv files take a long time to load into memory, they are unwieldy to maninpulate in R, they are difficult to read with csvkit (complicated header, adaptation data after column names), they are difficult to extract metadata from... if I load/subset, I have to reload each time I want a new subset of columns (also slow)... > set up to run Stan --- there are too many dependencies already.
> It could be optional in some way, which I guess R is OK with.

All Stan needs to do is hand over control over output by relying on callbacks. I could see two ways of doing it:

1) Create a Stan interface that relies on streaming everything (model, data, etc...) through protocol buffers (?) and provide the necessary callbacks as part of that interface. The result is another interface package, as independent of Stan/Math libraries as any other. A more reasonable goal might be to fork CmdStan just to experiment with how well streaming output to different databases works.

2) Make rstan's API (_NOT_ the regular interface) flexible enough to allow the programmer to pass in arbitrary callbacks. The result is another R package that's dependent on rstan.

I'm not saying either option is straightforward but with the current refactor I don't think it's outlandish either.

2) Make rstan's API (_NOT_ the regular interface) flexible enough to allow the programmer to pass in arbitrary callbacks.  The result is another R package that's dependent on rstan.

I'm not saying either option is straightforward but with the current refactor I don't think it's outlandish either.

Krzysztof
